record.title: The AI cost of JavaScript frameworks
record.author: luu
record.article_text: One of my pet peeves with the web development community is that so many of the decisions we make are vibes-based. Frameworks are “blazing fast,” tools will… One of my pet peeves with the web development community is that so many of the decisions we make are vibes-based. Frameworks are “blazing fast,” tools will “supercharge” your development, the right abstraction will benefit both you and your users ( DX and UX all in one!). All of this breathless boasting is usually offered with zero evidence. Alex Russell has called this “frontend’s lost decade” , Baldur Bjarnason has called programming a pop culture , and I’ve tried to counter this trend in my blog with facts and benchmarks (at my best, anyway). For a long time it seemed like our community’s allergy to evidence was driven by the desire for greater DX . In other words, devs just liked the way it felt to type JSX in React, and the arguments promoting React or related tools (“the virtual DOM is fast!”) were largely post-hoc rationalizations to justify those initial gut feelings. ( Jonathan Haidt would likely agree with this assessment.) But in the agentic era, when developers are no longer typing code by hand and are thus less constrained by DX, I still see vibes ruling the day (and not just in the sense of “vibe-coding”). Frontends are rewritten because some framework or another is “better for agents.” (Did anyone think to ask the agents?) The resulting code is “faster,” the agents make “fewer mistakes,” etc. Once again, these claims are often made without evidence. Whenever I read one of these accounts, I think to myself, “Where are the benchmarks?” Well I got curious, so I wrote a benchmark. The structure of this benchmark is pretty straightforward: The app is fairly simple: you’ve got a list of Pokémon with their types, moves, and data from various games. You can search, filter, etc.: I should start off with some caveats: this is not a perfect experiment. This app represents only one holotype – it’s a relatively content-based site with little interactivity, closer to a Wikipedia than a Figma, GMail, etc. That said, I had to choose some app to build, and this one is at least easy to understand at a high level, and relatively straightforward to spec out and test. To try to even the playing field, I had each framework/meta-framework use the official MCP or skills for that tool. I wanted to avoid accusations of “this framework is not well-represented in the training data, that’s why we built our MCP, we expect people to use it,” etc. I also didn’t over-specify the exact architecture to use (e.g. SSR vs CSR ), nor did I specify that the app should be as performant as possible. I simply gave the spec to Opus 5.5 with high effort and told it to use the latest version of the given framework. Each agent ran in a sandbox and without any knowledge that it would be tested in Lighthouse on performance and accessibility, although it was given the conformance test suite. Note I also didn’t mandate any CSS methodology, except to avoid using Tailwind, Bootstrap, or any other component framework, and to design based on a set of spec tokens to enforce some visual consistency. I didn’t want to make this test all about CSS, but instead about JS frameworks, CSR vs SSR, SPAs vs MPAs , etc. The resulting app is tested against a conformance suite based on the accessibility tree rather than the raw DOM to avoid mandating any particular HTML structure – one framework uses web components which rely on shadow DOM, so this was required. One thing I learned from this experiment is that everything I’m measuring is very stochastic. LLMs are random-word generators, so sometimes you get a low dice-roll and an agent goes off on some weird tangent wasting a bunch of tokens, through no fault of the framework or its tools. Lighthouse itself can give inconsistent results as well: Largest Contentful Paint (LCP) may decide that one image is the “largest” element, then pick another one on the next run. It’s hard to have a perfectly fair experiment, but running multiple iterations did help, and I’ve tried to be honest about the variance. With all that throat-clearing out of the way, let’s get to the results. I’m going to break this down by multiple dimensions: cost to build, quality, and maintainability. For each framework/meta-framework, I took the median of 5 runs: in other words, I built the same app 5 times in the same framework. (Yes, this is the kind of zany thing you can do with coding agents these days.) The exception was Angular, which failed to create a working app twice, so I took 3 iterations instead. (This is explained below.) Note that this quotes the API prices directly from Claude Code and doesn’t actually represent how much money I spent. I’m on a Max plan, so this was just part of my overall $100/month. Note also the variance: React Router’s median is roughly $1 worse than that of Hono+htmx, but the cheapest version of React Router ($2.82) is still cheaper than the most expensive version of Hono+htmx ($3.19). However some reliable patterns do emerge. Most clearly, SvelteKit, Gracile+Lit, and Angular are more expensive to build than the other frameworks. For SvelteKit, this may be due to the fact that the agents read the SvelteKit v3 migration guide in every run, likely because it’s too new to be in Opus 5.5’s training data. Similarly for Gracile, the agents didn’t know the framework very well and either cloned the Gracile repo or read its compiled source from node_modules . For Angular it seems to be a function of the total code size (see below). I should also mention that not every agent made use of an MCP/skill/Claude Code plugin, nor did every framework have one: For example, TanStack Start’s agent only discovered its skill files in 2/5 runs (they’re shipped in the node_modules of the project). For Nuxt, the MCP was never used by the agents. For Next.js, agents only read the skill file in 1/5 runs and the AGENTS.md in 2/5 runs. This is a wide range of results, which points back to the stochastic nature of LLMs. I still consider this a valid experiment, though, because I doubt many vibe-coders are shouting at their agents in all-caps to use the MCP (and plenty are probably skipping it entirely). Also, if you’re wondering how I came up with Hono+htmx: essentially, I wanted htmx represented somehow, and Hono seemed like a fine pairing (i.e. as a JavaScript alternative to Rails/Django/etc.). As for Gracile+Lit, I wanted web components represented via their standard-bearer framework (Lit), and was only aware of Gracile as a meta-framework. If there are better candidates, then those would be great for a follow-up experiment. For “Vanilla,” note that the agent was told to use “vanilla JavaScript or TypeScript with Vite, without a UI framework.” Surprisingly, this underperforms several frameworks, which seems to demonstrate that having some framework can be better than nothing (or better than raw Vite, anyway). Vite was chosen because it undergirds many frameworks and represents fairly standard and agnostic JavaScript infrastructure. The total time and tokens track pretty closely with the cost: Wall-clock minutes from the agent’s perspective. Median of 3-5 runs. The tokens, by the way, were reported by Claude Code. The duration is just the total wall-clock time. Of course, because I think that outcomes matter, I also tested the agents with Lighthouse. As software developers, I think it’s important that we not only build things cheaply but also performantly and accessibly. For simplicity’s sake, I’m only reporting the scores for the home page. There are other pages, but they all score fairly similarly or they have wild swings in metrics like LCP, so it just complicates things to include them. record.author: proy87
record.story_text:
Hello everyone. I’m a mathematician by training, and I love mathematical and logical puzzles and brain-teasers. Inspired by popular games like Sudoku and Wordle, I decided to come up with an engaging game of my own.

As it turns out, that’s not so easy! I had a few ideas, but beyond the core mechanics, a game also needs to be interesting and easy to explain — after all, nobody (including me) wants to spend a long time reading through rules.

Let’s start with the concept, which came to me quite spontaneously: what if we represented letters like the digits on a digital clock — using lines, with dots at the points where those lines intersect? For instance, the letter "E" would consist of four lines and six dots — three at the intersections and three at the ends of the lines.

It turns out that every letter of the Latin alphabet can be represented this way (with a minor caveat) using three rows of dots connected by some lines. This immediately presented a challenge: how do you represent O-shaped parts, like those found in "B", "O", or "R"? I decided not to use O-shapes, an use onl rectangles/squares. This "alphabet" is always displayed below the game board, so the player can see the letters.

The goal of the game is simple: you are presented with three rows of dots and a set of lines, and you have to figure out the word. A great feature of the game is that it’s possible to deduce the word in a single turn — all the necessary information is right there on the board, allowing you to arrive at the answer with certainty. And what if you can’t figure it out on the first try? You can enter a guess, much like in Wordle: if the lines from the entered word are part of the target word, they turn green; if not, they turn red. The same applies to the dots. As you play, more and more lines gradually appear...

Why provide some lines at the start? To uniquely identify a specific word — or a small set of words — from the dictionary. For example, you could select a configuration of lines that corresponds to only one word, like "RADIO", or perhaps to just two possible words, such as "WEIGH" and "WRONG".

The rules seem clear, but the mechanics — not so much. There are dots on the board; when I enter a word, I realize there aren't enough dots. What should I do? Initially, if the target word had 5 letters, I allowed users to enter 4- or 5-letter guesses, but that just confused players. So, I came up with a different solution: adding red dots for dots that aren't part of the target word.

Another drawback is that the game is somewhat skewed. Since letters are processed from left to right, the first letters are revealed more frequently than the last ones.

Then there’s the game design itself: should the target words be 5 letters long, or 6? Should a single board allow for multiple possible answers (like "WEIGH" and "WRONG"), or should it be limited to one — or perhaps more than two? Should the difficulty increase from Monday to Sunday? Currently, it’s set up this way: Monday is the easiest (a few 3-letter words), while Sunday is the hardest (more than two 7-letter words).

The tech stack is simple: I use Flask for the backend and Python for the algorithms; I wrote the algorithms myself. While the JS, HTML, and CSS were created with the help of AI.

I’d love for you to test the game and share what you like, what you don’t, and what could be improved.

Specifically, I’d like to know:

1. Is the game and its goal clear?

2. Is it fun to play, and what could be improved?

3. Would you share it with your friends?

I welcome any constructive criticism.

You can find the game at https://www.jointter.com/

It’s free and requires no registration.

Thank you very much.

text: Show HN: Overtone – Transcribe, correct and cut captions for any screen shape Reliable transcription, with captions cut for every screen shape from one file. An open caption format, a video.js plugin

record.title: Show HN: Overtone – Transcribe, correct and cut captions for any screen shape
record.author: rvanderlinden
record.story_text:
Hi HN, I'm Ruud, co-founder of Lont. We turn company emails into personalized videos.

Video captions cost us manual work twice: fixing misheard words, then fixing layout, like lines ending on “the”.

Overtone uses multiple models to listen to the audio: gpt-transcribe, Azure STT, and Elevenlabs Scribe. When they return conflicting results, Overtone sends small clips to the models again, and then lets an LLM decide what was actually said.

The LLM is like a human doing a sanity check on the transcription model. Humans would easily recognize a word to be different based on context. The LLM basically does the same, using an optional context prompt + its world knowledge. Because of this the Word Error Rate (WER) on many test files is lower when using Overtone, compared to just using a model without it.

Sure, the cost is higher because we use up to 3 different STT models + an LLM, but it still removes mistakes, reducing the time needed to fix captions to a minimum, and reducing the chance you'll miss something. For us it's worth it. For ultra high volume use cases it may not be.

The rules-based cutter nicely cuts the transcript into captions that look good, depending on screen size: 16:9 is different from 9:16, and the Overtone Format we created supports any type really. Pauses become breaks, captions are grouped per speaker, and names/numbers are never spread out over multiple captions.

How to add these captions to your videos? A videojs plugin can do this automatically, so you don't burn in your captions. The plugin lets you cycle between styled captions, plain captions, and off. You can burn them into an MP4 file with overtone burn.

Quickly try it out just the cutter? Try:

  npx overtone-captions recut yoursub.srt
Transcribing audio with API keys works too. Use --dry-run to show a cost estimate before you send.

We open-sourced this first version (MIT) because we believe many people can benefit from this, especially if your captions just need to be good. There's plenty of room to improve though, so we've made it easy to help contribute to add style packs, languages, and providers/models.

You can find a demo at: https://overtone.lont.ai/

Find the code and benchmarks here: https://github.com/lonthq/overtone-captions

An open caption format, a video.js plugin with style packs, and a CLI that recuts, burns in and exports word-timed ca... One .overtone.json file in a 16:9 and a 9:16 player ( social style pack), on the Blender open movie Tears of Steel. Film: (CC) Blender Foundation | mango.blender.org , CC BY 3.0 . Overtone stores each spoken word once, with its time and speaker, and cuts captions separately for each picture shape: 16:9 and 9:16 by default, or any aspect you name. A CLI makes the file from your subtitles, audio or video. A video.js plugin shows the cut that fits the player. Re-cut subtitles you already have. Offline, no API key, no ffmpeg (Node.js 22.12 or newer): You get TOS-en.overtone.json , .horizontal and .vertical .vtt and .srt files, and a transcript. Word times are estimated from the cues. Caption a video from its audio. This needs ffmpeg and provider API keys (OpenAI and Azure AI Speech by default; overtone providers lists the variables). --dry-run shows where the audio goes and the estimated cost, and sends nothing: Most captions are cut once, for one screen, by filling each line to a length limit. The 16:9 cut is too wide for a 9:16 phone video, lines end on "the" or "of", and two speakers share a caption. Overtone keeps a cut per screen shape in one file. The cuts follow reading rules: lines avoid ending on weak words, names and numbers stay together, each speaker gets their own caption, and pauses become line or caption breaks, so viewers who cannot hear a hesitation can read it. The same words and times from a NASA interview, cut for 9:16 (22 characters × 2 lines): Why a new format instead of WebVTT or TTML: those store finished cues, so a player can only rewrap them. .overtone.json stores each word once, plus any number of cuts that point to those words. Export WebVTT or SRT per cut when you need a standard file. Why not WhisperX, stable-ts or a hosted speech API: they give good words and times, often cheaper. Overtone adds the caption layout on top. overtone recut re-cuts their SRT or WebVTT output, so you can keep your engine. The LLM never sets timestamps: each word takes its time from the engines. By Jonathan O'Shea | 30 Oct 2026 16:50 , Last updated: 01 Nov 2026 11:42 Surprise leaders Lazio will look to prolong an incredible start to the Serie A season on Sunday, when they welcome Cagliari to Stadio Olimpico. For the first time since they last lifted the Scudetto, the Biancocelesti are unbeaten through their first nine league games; meanwhile, the visitors remain in Rome after suffering another defeat in midweek. With the Serie A summit up for grabs, Lazio briefly went top of the pile on Tuesday night, smashing 10-man Sassuolo 6-2 in Reggio Emilia. Tijjani Noslin bagged a brace as the Biancocelesti moved above reigning champions Inter Milan with yet another win, making it seven from eight games so far. Inter were soon back on top after winning in Venice, but they subsequently lost to city rivals AC Milan, and optimistic Lazio fans may even be eyeing a first title since the 1999-2000 campaign. Gennaro Gattuso will not entertain such talk, even though his team boast the division's best defensive record and have now scored at least twice in their last seven Serie A matches. That is the capital club's best such run since Simone Inzaghi's side reached 12 in 2020, when they were contending for the Scudetto until COVID-19 intervened. Lazio have also averaged above two goals per game while winning 13 of their last 14 games against Cagliari at Stadio Olimpico, where a fan boycott will leave most seats empty again this weekend. Home or away, Cagliari are winless in 22 Serie A matches against Lazio, dating back to 2013; furthermore, only February's goalless draw ended a streak of six consecutive defeats. Even more concerning is the Rossoblu's recent run of results, as their form has fallen off a cliff following a fast start to the current campaign. After winning four of their first six league fixtures, Cagliari have lost all of the next three, and they had failed to score for more than 250 minutes leading into Tuesday's clash with Roma. Before facing Lazio, Fabio Pisacane 's side took on the Biancocelesti’s city rivals at the Olimpico, and they came quite close to pulling off a shock. Having seized an early lead, they were trailing 2-1 until the 81st minute, when substitute Daniel Maldini dramatically levelled things up; however, Roma then struck back with two late goals. Without Europe to concern him, Gattuso has made relatively few changes so far, and it should be a settled Lazio side that takes to the field on Sunday - even if the hosts now have more options. Adam Marusic and Nicolo Rovella are both back from injury, and Andrea Pinamonti recovered from illness in time to face former club Sassuolo in midweek, so only Albert Gudmundsson is still sidelined. Noslin must beat Pinamonti to selection up front, but captain Mattia Zaccagni is a fixture on the Biancocelesti's left flank; now back to his best, the latter has seven Serie A goal involvements this term. Meanwhile, Maldini is Cagliari's form player: having scored two goals in 12 Lazio appearances last season, the Italy forward has netted five in his first nine for Cagliari. Pisacane will be missing long-term absentees Riyad Idrissi and Mattia Felici, but Harry Winks appears to have overcome a back problem. Young striker Yael Trepy returned to the pitch and almost scored against Roma, two months after nearly drowning and being placed in an induced coma. Mandas; Floriani Mussolini, Doekhi, Provstgaard, Tavares; Frattesi, Belahyane, Taylor; Isaksen, Noslin, Zaccagni Caprile; Ze Pedro, Mina, Rodriguez, Obert; Deiola, Winks; Romano, Adopo; Maldini, Mendy While Lazio cannot stop scoring, Cagliari have begun to leak goals at an alarming rate, and that is not a great combination for the Sardinian side. So, the hosts' success streak will go on, while the visitors are set for their second loss in Rome within the space of five days. record.title: Last-minute Halloween costumes for tech nerds
record.body: No Halloween costume? Just be a deceptively cute AI agent icon, a PHP vulnerability, or sleepy time Bryan Johnson. It happens to the best of us — you’ve completely dropped the ball on figuring out a Halloween costume. Naturally, you’ve decided to solve this problem by turning to… TechCrunch? Yeah, sure, why not. I’ve got some ideas. Here are some last-minute techy Halloween costumes. Effort levels vary. AI leaders like Dario Amodei and Sam Altman have expressed their fears that AI is developing too quickly , but if AI models become capable of “recursive self-improvement,” they’ll be able to advance on their own without human intervention, rendering any efforts to “pace the frontier” futile. I’m not sure how to visually represent the idea of an AI building itself, but you could really lean into the “self-improvement” part and forget the “recursive” aspect — it’s a last-minute Halloween costume. You don’t need to try that hard. Dress as the version of yourself you imagine becoming every year when you make New Year’s resolutions. Carry around a self-help or productivity book like “Atomic Habits” or anything by Malcolm Gladwell, a yoga mat, and a huge bottle of water. Leave in the middle of the party to “go to therapy” when you actually just want to go home. Brag to people about how good your Oura Ring’s sleep score is. You are the embodiment of someone trying to better themselves. You are recursive self-improvement. Meta and OpenAI both recently launched AI assistants with creepily cute avatars. It’s almost Elizabeth Holmes-esque — they look innocent, so you underestimate their potential to cause disaster. (While we’re talking about her, you’re only allowed to do the black turtleneck Holmes costume if you’re a natural blonde, or if you have a blonde wig.) What you’re going to do is make yourself look big and fluffy. Maybe you have a poofy puffer jacket, or maybe you can find some colorful feather boas to wrap yourself in. Add a distinctive hat, glasses, or other accessory to make yourself look more like a ChatGPT dot. If you have a colorful shirt and matching bottoms, that also works. Throughout the night, ask people if you can obtain read/write access to their Gmail. Whether you call them “pervert glasses” or not, we should all be able to agree that it would be really spooky if someone just started recording you without your consent — perfectly in keeping with the Halloween spirit. Just grab a pair of glasses — or buy a cheap pair somewhere convenient — and attach a big red or white circle to one lens, mimicking the red recording light. If you want to make the costume extra creepy (or, if you can’t make a big circle sticker), you can just wear normal glasses and say that you’re “guy recording with the light covered up.” Please, just don’t actually record people without their consent while you wear this costume. While we’re at it, Mark Zuckerberg’s fashion has been pretty recognizable lately. He’s been wearing a lot of slightly oversized, boxy black T-shirts. It may be hard to replicate the black-text-on-black-shirt style he gravitates toward, but you could attach a piece of paper to yourself that says “Building is my love language.” If you feel confident in your Latin pronunciation, you could go for something actually scary, like the time he wore a shirt that said “Aut Zuck aut nihil,” which means “Either Zuck or nothing.” It’s a little ominous. For some people, there’s nothing scarier than running out of Claude tokens. Grab a piece of cardboard, print out screenshots of notifications telling you that you’ve reached your usage limit, and go spook some vibe-coders. I’ve illustrated this idea using an edited stock photo. You don’t have to dress like you work at Hot Topic — that’s just the model in the image. The scary PHP-ocalypse is fresh in our memory — it was only last week that AI unearthed critical PHP flaws that could’ve been catastrophic for the internet. The fear that web developers felt is still palpable, making it a good Halloween costume: You are a PHP vulnerability. Here’s what you’re going to do. Buy a T-shirt and a sharpie, and write PHP on it. Keep it simple. What about the vulnerability part? You’re going to have to commit to the bit. All night, you’re going to talk to your friends about your feelings. Actually bare your emotions. Talk about how your recent loss of a loved one made you remember how fragile life can be. If making yourself vulnerable kills the vibe, just pretend it was part of the Halloween costume and that you’re really cool and fun and never feel sad ever. Maybe you have more than one Halloween party to go to this weekend, but you want your various costumes to stick to a specific theme. Once you’ve got your sleepy time getup sorted, it’s time to prep your second costume portraying the controversial biohacker : GLP-Bryan. Johnson wrote on X earlier this year: “I frequently lay on top of Kate with all of my bodyweight. The deep pressure calms her nervous system, quiets racing thoughts, and releases oxytocin which lowers cortisol. We call it GLP-Bryan.” Naturally, people were confused, so he shared an image to demonstrate. Yes, this will be hard to reproduce as a Halloween costume, but if you’ve run out of time to buy anything, this one will do. Just wear a T-shirt and jeans, which you probably already own. It will be weird to lie on top of your partner in the middle of a party. Really weird. But that’s what you get for waiting until now to figure out a costume. record.title: You don’t need to believe in a god to get a religious exemption from using AI at work
record.body: David Durman, a University of Kentucky administrator, recently earned a religious exemption from using AI in the workplace. Pope Leo XIV has decried AI as a threat to human dignity , but it’s not just the devoutly faithful who might worry about how AI squares with their beliefs. David Durman, a nontheistic humanist, recently secured a religious exemption from using AI in the workplace. “Humanism is a collection of beliefs about the human experience and how humans interact with the world,” Durman, a University of Kentucky administrator, told TechCrunch. It centers on “human well-being and flourishing, both individually and collectively … and implores a person to try to improve both their well-being and their flourishing as well as the others around them.” As he watched AI grow more popular in daily life, Durman sought out the American Humanist Association (AHA) — a nonprofit advancing secular humanism — to investigate how he could gain legal protections against having to use AI at work. He believes that using the technology runs counter to his beliefs. “The way we become moral actors for ourselves and for others is through the active application of our minds, and the diminishing of that [through AI use] is going to necessarily have a negative impact on our ability to do so,” he said, reflecting on how overreliance on AI might affect critical thinking. In a statement published by the AHA earlier this week, Durman wrote, “AI is interfering with people’s ability to earn a living, the environmental costs spell disaster for humanity and our planet, and its supplanting and theft of human creativity threaten elements of our culture like art and literature that make society flourish.” Humanism is not anti-religious, but it tends to appeal to people who are skeptical of a god or other supernatural power yet still seek a scientific and moral framework to ground themselves in. “Concern about AI and human dignity can run through several different faiths and traditions, whether that’s Catholic teachings, or Universalism, or Humanism, and we want Humanists or nontheists to know that they fall into these categories — that they are also protected by the law at work,” Alexandria Huiskens, staff attorney at the AHA, told TechCrunch. Durman is the first humanist to secure workplace accommodations that allow him to abstain from AI use, and one of the first people to publicly discuss their pursuit of these protections. He was inspired to seek them when he read that Erin Maus , a Unitarian Universalist and software engineer, was able to secure similar protections for herself. “For me, this was about me and my convictions,” Durman said. “I’m obviously not trying to tell people how to think or feel … But I do hope that it encourages people who have similar concerns to pursue not necessarily religious exemption, but pursue their concerns to the best of their ability where they feel is the most appropriate.” University of Kentucky spokesperson Jay Blanton told TechCrunch that the institution reviews requests for religious accommodations on an individual basis, considering the employee’s job responsibilities and the circumstances of the request. “In this case, the university determined that an accommodation could be provided while allowing the employee to continue performing the essential functions of their position,” Blanton said in a statement. “As technology and job responsibilities evolve, accommodations may be reviewed to ensure they remain reasonable and workable.” Maus’ situation is especially unusual, since it has become rare for software engineers to write code without any AI assistance. But in Durman’s administrative role, in which he supports researchers applying for grants, he has not been required to use AI at work. Like many workers across fields, some of his colleagues and leadership have recommended that employees try out these tools, so he sought to secure his exemption now, in case the suggestion becomes a mandate in the future. “I hope that if [others] have similar feelings, that they feel encouraged to pursue some kind of resolution,” Durman said. text: I Spent 30 Minutes With Apple’s CEO. Now I Know Why John Ternus Got the Job Apple doesn’t need fixing, and it doesn’t want drama. Its new leader is a “product guy” who bleeds six colors. The brief cer

record.title: I Spent 30 Minutes With Apple’s CEO. Now I Know Why John Ternus Got the Job
record.body: Apple doesn’t need fixing, and it doesn’t want drama. Its new leader is a “product guy” who bleeds six colors. The brief ceremony introducing the new Macbook Pro this week was as low-key as the presenter, Apple’s new CEO John Ternus. He stepped onto the low stage at a Los Angeles event space with zero fanfare, said hi, and queued up a video showing the first touchscreen Mac. Then he released the modest crowd of journalists and creators to get hands-on with the new laptop and roam between eye-popping demos of music producers, filmmakers, photographers, and fashion designers using the laptop. Ternus, who at 51 is on the younger side of Apple’s top management, has been CEO for less than two months. But this launch and a series of other recent announcements have made one thing clear. With this new guy—if a 25-year Apple veteran could be considered new—it’s all about the products. Perhaps fittingly, the biggest noise of the presentation came when Ternus revealed that the new device restores the illumination to the Apple logo. Maybe that’s a symbol that in the age of AI, Apple is beaming out the message that hardware still rules. A few minutes after the presentation, I sat down with Ternus, for the second time in two days. Steve Jobs used to grant me an audience after his famous keynotes, too. Ternus isn’t Jobs, of course, nor is he supposed to be. But who is he? I first met Ternus in 2015, when I spent a day with him at Apple’s Input Design Lab, a testing facility in Cupertino. He’d risen to VP for Mac, iPad, Ecosystem, and Audio Engineering, and he struck me as affable and knowledgeable. (He spent four years right out of college at a virtual reality company, but he’s been at Apple ever since.) The peg to my story at the time was how this unknown manager conducted a Javert-like investigation to fix the weird sound a redesigned mouse made when sliding on a table. That attention to detail was a legacy of Jobs’ perfectionism, which Tim Cook sustained as the next CEO. In the decade when Ternus overlapped with Jobs, he says he had only “a handful of interactions” with the founder. “But I've always felt like sort of a student of Steve's teachings,” Ternus said. “And then being able to work very closely with Tim, I’ve been very lucky.” Ternus has so far been defined by his product prowess. “John innately has a great sense for great products, and that’s what Apple is,” says Greg Joswiak, Apple’s SVP of worldwide marketing and a 40-year company veteran. “You can’t teach that.” In one sense Ternus’ ascension is similar to that of Microsoft’s Satya Nadella, another lifer promoted to the top post. But Nadella was called upon to fix a broken organization, while Apple has been on a multi-decade run. Ternus is explicit that he will be an engine of continuity . That word is key to his selection, and above all explains why Tim Cook and the rest of Apple’s board was so comfortable with the choice. The extent to which Ternus is a deep Apple insider became clear when I probed him on his views on being a corporate leader. I asked him which non-Apple CEOs he admires, and he was stumped. “I haven't really thought about that,” he said. I asked whether any business books had an impact on him. “Not really,” he said. “Of course I’ve read books, but there's so much to be learned from the people I get to work with.” Indeed, every time I tried to pin down Ternus on what mark he wants to make at Apple, he deflected the question and told me how he will continue Apple’s commitment to internal collaboration. Ternus’ key collaborator is probably Johny Srouji, the architect of the company’s custom silicon, an initiative that’s driven many of the company’s innovations in the past decade. Srouri says that their relationship will be even closer, as Apple has merged its hardware engineering and technology organizations with Srouji at the top, reporting to Ternus. “John is going to be a great CEO,” he said. “He's a product guy at heart, but Apple's secret weapon is the DNA, the culture, which is not going to change. Remember, John has been here for 25 years. It’s not like he's going to come and everything's going to be different.” Being Apple’s CEO encompasses much more than products—there’s a $100 billion business in services, a huge infrastructure, and the general mishegoss of running a giant corporation. I asked Ternus what it’s like to take on a massively expanded portfolio. “One of the amazing privileges of this job is getting to learn so many new things,” he said. “I have been and will continue to learn and go deeper into different areas. But, you know, I do love product. I'm super passionate about it.” Like it or not, the CEO of a $4 trillion company has to be involved in policy and politics. It has been widely reported that as executive chair, Cook will still conduct some of Apple’s high-level policy duties, including the equivalent of stuffing gold-plated binkies in the presidential mouth. Ternus implies that the reality is more nuanced. “Tim is available to help wherever I ask him, and it's great to have him in that role,” he said. “He obviously has a ton of relationships he's developed over the years, and of course, I'm building new relationships in this role as well.” One relationship he has yet to build: the president. Ternus has yet to meet Donald Trump. Then there’s the one thing that could possibly disrupt the way Apple has run its business for the past 50 years. Ternus is taking over the company during what may be the biggest technological shift ever. I suggested to Ternus that history may judge him on how he handles AI . I spelled out for him a couple of narratives people spin about Apple. One is that Apple has been hobbled by a failure to develop its AI product Siri, and even after an update it’s still in catch-up mode. The other is that Apple is smart to avoid the high cost of developing a frontier model and that the strategy of organically putting AI into its products, with a focus on privacy, will pay off in the long run. “Everyone has an opinion—I really like where we’re at,” he said. “I would hope people recognize that the work we do is building incredible products that make their lives better. We’re absolutely going to leverage AI to do that. We don't want to ship AI for AI's sake. When we're doing it right, people won’t have to think about whether it was AI that made this happen or more traditional software. What matters is, did we build something that they really love?” That assumes that AI, as powerful as it is, will wind up as a “normal” technology, organically integrated into our current gadget-sphere. Another school of thought is that AI is an apocalyptic disruptor that will shred the current ecosystem. In that vision, all those cool apps Apple supports will be subsumed by AI-concocted agents generated from prompts, or even autonomously. Ternus doesn’t buy that scenario. “That could make life really easy, I suppose, but the creation of products is a deeply human and personal thing, something that we love to do,” he said. When I asked whether he’s in favor of AI regulation, he replied, “We all read the stories and think about it from a cybersecurity standpoint—clearly these models are very capable of doing things. Our focus is on making sure that our products are secure and safe, and protecting the users' information.” His non-answer shows that he might well be on the way to mastering political communication. But policy will never be the focus of John Ternus. He is, and probably always will be, the product-guy CEO. Before we ended our conversation, Ternus had one question for me: “What did you think of the logo?” This is an edition of Steven Levy’s and Lauren Goode's Backchannel newsletter .
